newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: More good news for opposition in Irish poll.
newsitem.headline: More good news for opposition in Irish poll.

text.p: Ireland's opposition Fianna Fail and Progressive Democrats alliance has doubled its lead over the government coalition with just over a week to go before elections, an opinion poll showed on Wednesday.
The poll put fresh confidence into the centre-right opposition alliance which has been consistently ahead of Prime Miniser John Bruton's government in every survey carried out for the past month.
The IMS survey, published in the Irish Independent newspaper, showed that Bertie Ahern's Fianna Fail and the Progressive Democrats are eight points ahead of Bruton's left-right "Rainbow coalition."
The alliance is seen as a centre-right alternative to the government, an untried partnership which Bruton cobbled together when the last government collapsed at the end of 1994.
The opposition lead was double what it was shown to have at the weekend and confirmed the opposition as the first choice among voters for the June 6 poll.

Thirty-eight per cent of voters said they would choose a party in the ruling coalition while 46 percent said they would back the opposition alliance, with 16 per cent saying they would choose parties outside the two main blocs.
The poll added weight to forecasts that neither of the two main blocs would score an outright victory and would have to bring in a junior partner to form a government.
The campaign has had a slightly negative bias on financial markets and analysts believe a long period of political bargaining that would follow a hung parliament could unsettle markets further.
The smaller parties include the Greens, whose support is stable at four per cent, and Sinn Fein, the political wing of Northern Ireland's Irish Republican Army guerrillas.

Sinn Fein polls around two per cent of votes in Irish elections and has no member of parliament but is confident that it can return at least one legislator from the border constituency of Monaghan and Cavan. The main loser appeared to be the Labour party in the ruling coalition with Bruton's Fine Gael and the small Democratic Left grouping.
The poll showed Labour's support dropping four popularity points to 10 per cent while most of the other major parties remain fairly stable.
Labour, led by Foreign Minister Dick Spring, pulled out of a Fianna Fail-led government in late 1994 and switched its 30 parliamentary seats, its biggest ever showing, to Bruton.
It held the balance of power in both governments but its influence would be dramatically cut if it wins only 20 seats in the elction, as some polls predict.
The election is being fought on the lines of an auction with each party capping the promises of its rivals on taxation, job creation and the fight against crime.

Law and Order has became a key issue since the unsolved murder last June of journalist Veronica Guerin, who was shot dead by suspected contract killers while investigating the lives of drug barons operating out of Ireland.
